title: Practice: List Operations & Filtering
summary: Put theory into practice with essential industry list manipulation patterns: in-place filtering, element transformation, deduplication, sublists, and multi-criteria sorting.
learningObjectives: Perform in-place element removal safely using Java 8+ Collection.removeIf()
Transform all list elements in-place using List.replaceAll()
Work with subList() views safely without triggering ConcurrentModificationException
Distinguish between Arrays.asList(), List.of(), and new ArrayList<>() initialization strategies
expectedOutcomes: Practical fluency writing production-grade list algorithms for data filtering, partitioning, and validation
Ability to avoid the dangerous pitfalls of unmodifiable list views and shared sublist references

analogy.headline: Inspecting, transforming, and filtering defective parts along an automated assembly line
analogy.story:
Imagine a factory assembly line producing precision electronic components.

As components glide down the conveyor belt:
1. **Filtering (`removeIf`)**: An optical sensor spots scratched components and kicks them off the belt immediately. No manual counting or shifting required.
2. **Transformation (`replaceAll`)**: A laser engraves a compliance serial code onto every single item that passes inspection.
3. **Inspection Window (`subList`)**: A quality-assurance inspector places a magnifying frame over 5 consecutive items on the belt. The inspector does not pick them up or duplicate them; they look directly through the frame window at the live belt.
4. **Batch Packaging (Chunking)**: Once verified, the components are packed into neat batches of 10 for shipment.

In Java, **`List`** provides all of these built-in assembly-line operations natively!
analogy.keyTakeaway: Modern Java Lists provide rich functional methods (removeIf, replaceAll, subList) to filter, transform, and partition data in-place with minimal boilerplate.

activities.title: Modern List Engineering: Essential Methods & Patterns

keyTakeaways: `removeIf(Predicate<E> filter)` mutates the list in-place in linear O(N) time with a single backward shift pass
`replaceAll(UnaryOperator<E> operator)` transforms every element without allocating new container objects
`subList(fromIndex, toIndex)` returns a live VIEW into the parent list, NOT an independent copy
`List.of()` creates an immutable list; `Arrays.asList()` creates a fixed-size mutable list; `new ArrayList<>()` creates a fully mutable list

activities.content:
### 1. In-Place Filtering: `removeIf`

Prior to Java 8, filtering elements from a list required manual iterator loops. Java 8 introduced `Collection.removeIf(Predicate)`:
```java
List<Integer> numbers = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(10, 15, 20, 25, 30));
// Remove all odd numbers in-place:
numbers.removeIf(n -> n % 2 != 0);
// numbers is now: [10, 20, 30]
```
`removeIf` operates in $O(n)$ time using a compact two-pointer shift algorithm inside `ArrayList`, outperforming manual loops.

### 2. In-Place Transformation: `replaceAll`

Instead of allocating a brand new list and copying transformed items:
```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("alice", "bob", "charlie"));
names.replaceAll(String::toUpperCase);
// names is now: [ALICE, BOB, CHARLIE]
```

### 3. The `subList(from, to)` Contract

`list.subList(int fromIndex, int toIndex)` returns a **view** of the portion of the list between `fromIndex` (inclusive) and `toIndex` (exclusive):
```text
Parent List: [A, B, C, D, E, F]
                     ^        ^
               fromIndex=2  toIndex=5
Sublist View:       [C, D, E]
```

> **CRITICAL WARNING**: Any structural modification (e.g. `add()` or `remove()`) to the parent list directly invalidates the `subList`! Subsequent calls on the sublist will immediately throw **`ConcurrentModificationException`**.

To make an independent copy that is safe from parent modifications:
```java
List<String> independentCopy = new ArrayList<>(parentList.subList(2, 5));
```

### 4. Creation Patterns: The Big Three

| Initialization Method | Mutability | Resizability | Null Elements Permitted? |
|---|---|---|:---:|
| `new ArrayList<>()` | Fully Mutable | Resizable (`add`, `remove`) | Yes |
| `Arrays.asList("A", "B")` | Elements Mutable (`set` works) | **Fixed Size** (`add`/`remove` throw `UnsupportedOperationException`) | Yes |
| `List.of("A", "B")` (Java 9+) | **Completely Immutable** | Fixed Size | **No (throws NPE)** |

questions.prompt: What happens if you invoke 'list.add("C")' on a list created with 'Arrays.asList("A", "B")'?
questions.explanation: Arrays.asList() returns a fixed-size wrapper backed directly by the array. Structural modifications like add() or remove() throw UnsupportedOperationException.

questions.prompt: What happens if you pass a null value to 'List.of("A", null, "C")' in Java 9+?
options: Replaces null with an empty string
questions.explanation: List.of() strictly disallows null elements and throws NullPointerException at creation time.

questions.prompt: What happens to a subList view if you structurally add an element to the parent list after creating the subList?
options: The subList automatically updates its bounds
The subList becomes completely severed from the parent
Any subsequent operation on the subList throws ConcurrentModificationException
questions.explanation: The subList contract states that structural modifications to the backing list make the semantics of the sublist undefined. In OpenJDK, it checks modCount and throws ConcurrentModificationException.

hints.hint: Structural changes to parent list desynchronize the sublist view.

questions.prompt: How can you safely clear a range of elements (e.g. from index 2 to 5) from an ArrayList?
options: Using a while loop with list.remove(2)
questions.explanation: The idiomatic Java way to remove a range from a list is list.subList(from, to).clear(). The clear() call mutates the backing list directly.

hints.hint: subList provides a view, and clear() on the view removes those elements from the parent!

questions.prompt: Which method signature in Java 8 allows filtering out elements matching a condition in-place?
questions.explanation: Collection.removeIf(Predicate<? super E> filter) removes all elements that satisfy the given predicate in-place.

options: Creates and returns a brand new list with trimmed strings
Mutates every element in the existing list in-place by applying the trim function
Throws an exception if strings are immutable
questions.explanation: List.replaceAll(UnaryOperator<E> operator) replaces each element of the list with the result of applying the operator to that element in-place.

questions.prompt: What does 'list.indexOf(o)' return if the object is NOT present in the list?
questions.explanation: Like String.indexOf(), list.indexOf(o) returns -1 if the specified element is not found.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended modern idiom to create a truly independent, mutable copy of an existing collection?
questions.explanation: The copy constructor 'new ArrayList<>(existingCollection)' creates a decoupled, mutable ArrayList populated with references from the source collection.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of 'Collections.sort(List<T> list)' on an ArrayList?
questions.explanation: Collections.sort() uses TimSort (an adaptive hybrid of MergeSort and InsertionSort), which operates in O(N log N) time in the average and worst case.

questions.prompt: How does 'subList(fromIndex, toIndex)' behave regarding the boundaries?
options: fromIndex is inclusive, toIndex is exclusive
Both fromIndex and toIndex are inclusive
Both fromIndex and toIndex are exclusive
fromIndex is exclusive, toIndex is inclusive
questions.explanation: Like String.substring(), subList(from, to) is half-open: fromIndex is inclusive, and toIndex is exclusive [from, to).

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between Arrays.asList(), List.of(), and new ArrayList<>()?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Arrays.asList() returns a fixed-size list backed by the array (elements can be modified via set(), but add/remove throw UnsupportedOperationException). List.of() (Java 9+) returns a completely immutable, null-hostile list (any mutation throws UnsupportedOperationException, and null elements throw NPE). new ArrayList<>() creates a fully mutable, resizable collection that permits nulls.
keyPoints: Arrays.asList: fixed-size, elements mutable, permits null
new ArrayList: fully mutable and resizable

interviewQA.question: How does subList() work, and why does mutating the parent list invalidate it?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: subList() returns a live view of the backing list rather than a new copy. It stores an offset and size, delegating all reads and writes directly to the parent list. If the parent list is structurally modified (add/remove) directly, its modCount increments. The subList detects this discrepancy on subsequent calls and throws ConcurrentModificationException to prevent corrupt views.
keyPoints: subList is a view, not a new list allocation
Shares underlying storage with parent list
Structural modification to parent causes ConcurrentModificationException

interviewQA.question: How do you remove elements matching a condition from a List in Java 8+ without throwing ConcurrentModificationException?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: You should use Collection.removeIf(Predicate). It is specifically optimized to remove elements in-place safely in a single pass without throwing ConcurrentModificationException. Alternatively, you can use an explicit Iterator and call iterator.remove().
keyPoints: Or use Iterator it = list.iterator() with it.remove()
Never remove directly from list inside an enhanced for-each loop

interviewQA.question: How does Collection.removeIf() achieve better performance than an explicit iterator loop?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: In ArrayList, removeIf is overridden to use a BitSet to track matching indices in a first pass, followed by a single compacted memory shift pass in a second pass. This shifts all remaining elements forward in one O(N) sweep rather than executing multiple O(N) System.arraycopy shifts for every deleted element.
keyPoints: Single memory shift pass avoids repeated array copies

interviewQA.question: How do you remove duplicates from an ArrayList while preserving the original insertion order?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: You can wrap the ArrayList in a LinkedHashSet (which enforces uniqueness while preserving insertion order), and then copy it back into an ArrayList: 'List<T> unique = new ArrayList<>(new LinkedHashSet<>(list));'. Alternatively, in Java 8+ streams: 'list.stream().distinct().collect(Collectors.toList());'.
keyPoints: Use LinkedHashSet to deduplicate and preserve order
HashSet does not preserve insertion order

interviewQA.question: How do you partition a large List of N items into smaller batches of size K (e.g. for batch SQL queries)?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: You can iterate with a stride of K: 'for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i += K)', and extract each batch using 'list.subList(i, Math.min(i + K, list.size()))'. In third-party libraries, Guava provides 'Lists.partition(list, K)', but in standard Java, subList() achieves this with zero memory overhead.
keyPoints: Extract batch: list.subList(i, Math.min(i + K, list.size()))

activities.title: Lesson 6 Mastery Checkpoint
checklist: I can filter lists in-place using removeIf() with lambda expressions.
I know how to transform elements in-place using replaceAll().
I understand that subList() is a view and know why parent mutations break it.
I know the exact differences between Arrays.asList(), List.of(), and new ArrayList<>().
I can partition large lists into fixed-size batches using subList.

practiceProblems.title: Safe In-Place Transaction Filter
practiceProblems.description: Filter out cancelled or zero-value transactions in-place using Collection.removeIf().
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Write a transaction audit cleaner:

1. In `Main.main()`:
   - Create a mutable `List<String> transactions = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(
       "TX_SUCCESS_100", "TX_CANCELLED_50", "TX_SUCCESS_0", "TX_SUCCESS_250", "TX_CANCELLED_90"
     ));`
   - Using `transactions.removeIf(...)`, remove all transactions that contain `"CANCELLED"` OR end with `"_0"`.
   - Print remaining transactions:
     `Valid Transactions: <list>`

practiceProblems.title: Batch Pagination Chunker
practiceProblems.description: Partition an arbitrary list of items into fixed-size sublist batches using a loop stride.
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Implement a batch partitioning algorithm:

1. In `Main` class:
   - Write static method:
     `public static <T> List<List<T>> partition(List<T> list, int batchSize)`
   - Split `list` into batches of at most `batchSize` using `list.subList(i, Math.min(i + batchSize, list.size()))`.

2. In `Main.main()`:
   - Create a list with numbers 1 to 7: `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]`.
   - Call `partition(numbers, 3)`.
   - Print each batch:
     `Batch 1: [1, 2, 3]`
     `Batch 2: [4, 5, 6]`
     `Batch 3: [7]`
practiceProblems.hint: Loop with for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i += batchSize) and use subList.

practiceProblems.title: Preserve-Order Duplicate Remover
practiceProblems.description: Deduplicate an ArrayList while strictly maintaining the first-occurrence insertion order.
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Deduplicate a list without losing original order:

1. In `Main.main()`:
   - Input list: `["Java", "Python", "Java", "C++", "Python", "Rust", "Java"]`.
   - Eliminate duplicates using a `LinkedHashSet`.
   - Re-wrap into an `ArrayList<String>`.
   - Print original count, deduplicated count, and clean list:
     `Original Count: 7`
     `Unique Count: 4`
     `Clean Roster: [Java, Python, C++, Rust]`
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Original Count: 7
Unique Count: 4
Clean Roster: [Java, Python, C++, Rust]
practiceProblems.hint: LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order and eliminates duplicates: new ArrayList<>(new LinkedHashSet<>(inputList)).

practiceProblems.title: Fix ConcurrentModificationException on SubList
practiceProblems.description: Fix a runtime ConcurrentModificationException caused by mutating the backing list during sublist processing.
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
A developer wrote code to inspect the top 3 users and then add an admin user to the list:
```java
List<String> users = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "Dave"));
List<String> top3 = users.subList(0, 3);
users.add("Admin"); // MUTATING PARENT LIST DIRECTLY!
System.out.println("Top 3: " + top3); // CRASHES with ConcurrentModificationException!
```

Your Task:
1. Fix the bug by creating an independent, decoupled copy of the sublist view.
2. In `Main.main()`, verify that `top3` can be safely printed even after adding `"Admin"` to `users`.
3. Output format:
   `Top 3: [Alice, Bob, Charlie]`
   `Total Users: 5`
practiceProblems.hint: Decouple the sublist: List<String> top3 = new ArrayList<>(users.subList(0, 3));
hints: Passing users.subList to new ArrayList<>() copies the elements into an independent buffer.
Parent additions will no longer affect top3.

practiceProblems.title: Top-K Leaderboard Window
practiceProblems.description: Maintain a dynamic leaderboard that keeps only the top 3 highest scores using Collections.sort and subList.
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a leaderboard window:

1. Define class `Leaderboard`:
   - `private final List<Integer> scores = new ArrayList<>();`
   - `public void addScore(int score)`: Appends `score`, sorts in descending order using `Collections.sort(scores, Collections.reverseOrder())`, and trims excess elements so `scores.size() <= 3` using `subList(3, scores.size()).clear();`.
   - `public void display()`: Prints `Top Scores: <scores>`.

2. In `Main.main()`:
   - Add scores: 450, 890, 320, 950, 600, 1020.
   - Call `display()`.
   - Output: `Top Scores: [1020, 950, 890]`
practiceProblems.hint: Sort descending with Collections.sort(scores, Collections.reverseOrder()). If scores.size() > 3, call scores.subList(3, scores.size()).clear().
